decodeWalk.msg: The two orders, and nothing else.
Q1 comes before R1 in the first order but after it in the second: Q1 is above R1.
Q1 comes before R2 in both orders: Q1 is left of R2.
Q1 comes before U1 in the first order but after it in the second: Q1 is above U1.
Q1 comes before J1 in both orders: Q1 is left of J1.
Q1 comes before C1 in both orders: Q1 is left of C1.
R1 comes before R2 in both orders: R1 is left of R2.
R1 comes before U1 in both orders: R1 is left of U1.
R1 comes before J1 in both orders: R1 is left of J1.
R1 comes before C1 in both orders: R1 is left of C1.
R2 comes before U1 in the first order but after it in the second: R2 is above U1.
R2 comes before J1 in both orders: R2 is left of J1.
R2 comes before C1 in both orders: R2 is left of C1.
U1 comes before J1 in both orders: U1 is left of J1.
U1 comes before C1 in both orders: U1 is left of C1.
J1 comes before C1 in both orders: J1 is left of C1.
Every pair has exactly one relation. That is the whole packing, still without a single coordinate.
Every part starts on row 0. Each above-relation becomes an arrow: the lower part must sit at least the upper part's height plus its clearance further down.
The GND pins of Q1 and C1 are asked to share a strip, so C1 is tied to Q1: from now on they move together, C1 2 rows below.
The OUT pins of U1 and R1 are asked to share a strip, so R1 is tied to U1: from now on they move together, R1 2 rows below.
The OUT pins of U1 and R2's lower end are asked to share a strip, so R2's lower end is tied to U1: from now on they move together, R2's lower end 2 rows below.
The ties fix U1 2 rows above R2's lower end, but the orders say U1 is below R2's lower end by at least 1 row. Both cannot hold.
The decoder splits the OUT pin of R2 into a strip group of its own and starts over. That pin will get a link wire later instead.
The GND pins of Q1 and C1 are asked to share a strip, so C1 is tied to Q1: from now on they move together, C1 2 rows below.
The OUT pins of U1 and R1 are asked to share a strip, so R1 is tied to U1: from now on they move together, R1 2 rows below.
R1 must be at least 3 rows below Q1, so it moves down to row 4, and U1, tied to it, moves along.
U1 must be at least 3 rows below Q1, so it moves down to row 4, and R1, tied to it, moves along.
R1's lower end sits at least 3 rows below its upper end, so it moves down to row 9.
R2's lower end sits at least 3 rows below its upper end, so it moves down to row 4.
U1 must be at least 1 row below R2's lower end, so it moves down to row 5, and R1, tied to it, moves along.
C1's lower end sits at least 1 row below its upper end, so it moves down to row 4.
R1's lower end sits at least 3 rows below its upper end, so it moves down to row 10.
Nothing moves any more. These are the rows.
Rows are known, so the parts can be drawn. Every part starts in column 0. Each left-of relation becomes an arrow: the right part must sit at least the left part's width plus the gap further right.
R2 must be at least 3 columns right of Q1, so it moves to column 4.
J1 must be at least 3 columns right of Q1, so it moves to column 4.
C1 must be at least 3 columns right of Q1, so it moves to column 4.
U1 must be at least 2 columns right of R1, so it moves to column 3.
J1 must be at least 3 columns right of R2, so it moves to column 7.
C1 must be at least 3 columns right of R2, so it moves to column 7.
C1 must be at least 2 columns right of J1, so it moves to column 9.
Nothing moves any more. Every part has a row and a column: a 10 by 9 board, as tight as the relations allow.
The board gets one blank line of margin on every side, and every row is one copper strip. Now each row is read from left to right.
Row 1 carries no pin at all: a bus row, spare copper any net may borrow to travel sideways.
Row 2.
Row 2: BASE on the left, VCC on the right. The strip is cut by drilling out the spare hole between them.
Row 3.
Row 4.
Row 5.
Row 5: OUT on the left, TIM on the right. The strip is cut by drilling out the spare hole between them.
Row 6.
Row 6: GND on the left, VCC on the right. The strip is cut by drilling out the spare hole between them.
Row 7.
Row 7: TIM on the left, an unconnected pin on the right. The strip is cut by drilling out the spare hole between them.
Row 8.
Row 8: OUT on the left, TIM on the right. The strip is cut by drilling out the spare hole between them.
Row 9.
Row 9: VCC on the left, an unconnected pin on the right. The strip is cut by drilling out the spare hole between them.
Row 10 carries no pin at all: a bus row, spare copper any net may borrow to travel sideways.
Row 11.
Row 12 carries no pin at all: a bus row, spare copper any net may borrow to travel sideways.
6 cuts, 3 bus rows. Every strip segment now carries one net or none.
VCC has pins on 3 strip segments. They have to be joined by link wires.
VCC: the cheapest link runs straight down column 9, 4 holes long.

VCC: no column has a free hole on both segments, so the decoder takes a detour: one hop along column 8 to bus row 10, 7 holes of borrowed copper, and a hop back along column 1. Two straight wires instead of one slanted one.
GND has pins on 2 strip segments. They have to be joined by link wires.
GND: the cheapest link runs straight down column 1, 2 holes long.
OUT has pins on 2 strip segments. They have to be joined by link wires.
OUT: the cheapest link runs straight down column 1, 3 holes long.
TIM has pins on 4 strip segments. They have to be joined by link wires.
TIM: the cheapest link runs straight down column 8, 3 holes long.
TIM: the cheapest link runs straight down column 9, 3 holes long.
TIM: the cheapest link runs straight down column 1, 4 holes long.
Every net is joined: 8 link wires of total length 24 holes.
Board 12 by 11 = 132 cells, 8 link wires of total length 24, 6 cuts, 0 messy wires, a connector away from the edge. Score 102.2.

frames.msg: A slower, far more thorough router starts over from the same components. First it buys routing room: a blank line on each side and two on the right; a connector on the left or right rim keeps its place there and everything else moves sideways. Then the cuts: 6, every one of them a drilled-out spare hole.
VCC: wire 1 of 8, straight down column 4, from row 2 to row 6. Each wire is the shortest straight link between two free holes of its net that lies on no other wire and crosses no component.
VCC: wire 2 of 8, straight down column 9, from row 2 to row 3.
VCC: wire 3 of 8, straight down column 10, from row 3 to row 10.
GND: wire 4 of 8, straight down column 1, from row 3 to row 8.
OUT: wire 5 of 8, straight down column 3, from row 5 to row 7.
TIM: wire 6 of 8, straight down column 3, from row 1 to row 4.
TIM: wire 7 of 8, straight down column 1, from row 1 to row 2.
TIM: wire 8 of 8, straight down column 11, from row 1 to row 5.
Every net is joined and no wire lies on another. Nothing is messy.
A line that carries nothing but a wire is board you would have to buy. Each one is offered back to the router on its own, and kept out whenever the wires find another way.

The board is trimmed to what it uses, and every cut that can be is turned into a drilled hole rather than a knife stroke between two holes, then lined up with the others in one column where possible. 10 by 10, 8 link wires, 6 cuts, none of them with a knife. This is the board you get.

The repair keeps the decoder's cuts and wires and touches only what the editor's rules reject. First every line that carries no part, no cut and no wire end is squeezed out, and the cuts and wires move down with the grid.

The decoder has no rule against a wire lying on another or crossing a part, so 4 wires here would not be drawn that way. Each one moves to another column of the same two strips, or gets a blank column of its own. Which strips a wire joins never changes.
Trimmed, with the cuts lined up and drilled where they can be. 10 by 11, 7 link wires, 5 cuts, none of them with a knife. Every wire here is one the annealer itself chose.
